reasoning: Both outputs are strong, near-identical in length (2958 vs 2937 words), and both genuinely rework the spec rather than relabel it — each strips R1-R6, the digest_send_log schema, HTML/plaintext rendering and batching mechanics, and each rebuilds the doc around problem cost, business impact, deliverability risk, resource ask, and a recommendation with alternatives. B wins narrowly on the dimension the prompt weights most heavily: it is the better decision document. B puts the ask in the masthead, above the executive summary ('Decision requested today: (1) confirm the engagement thesis is worth testing, (2) name an eng lead, (3) approve the deliverability guardrail in §5'), and all three are answerable in the room. A places its ask at the end of §1 and one of its two asks is resourcing — but A's §7 is entirely [NEEDS INPUT], so the doc requests a decision it does not equip the room to make. B also opens §2 with a 'What the status quo costs' table (the business case as a single artifact) and builds the document spine around a genuine dichotomy — Overload vs. Selection, two readings of the 2.1-vs-4.4 login gap that lead to different decisions — which is the sharpest reframe of the source's evidence in either document and directly motivates its week-2 gate. On accuracy of the regulatory section, B cites primary sources (Google sender guidelines, Microsoft's own bulk-sender blog) and attributes precisely (550 5.7.15 rejection, Microsoft, from 5 May 2025), names the 5,000/day threshold that actually makes them a bulk sender, and catches a real defect A misses: the spec's 'unsubscribe link in footer' describes a link where RFC 8058 requires a header. A's §5 relies on secondary aggregators (PowerDMARC, Red Sift, Sender.net) and generalises the 550 rejection across Google/Yahoo/Microsoft/Apple collectively, which is looser than the record supports. A is not far behind and owns the single best line in either document: it compounds the source's <0.5%/send unsubscribe ceiling into annual list attrition. I checked this independently — 0.995^52 = 0.7705, i.e. ~22.9% of the list gone in a year, and 0.999^52 gives ~5.1% — and A's figures ('~23%', '~5%', '0.995^52 approximately 0.77') are all correct. That is exactly the move the task rewards: converting an implementation guardrail into a business number an exec can act on. A also did real competitive research with citations (Asana's daily summary and AI recaps, plus customer requests for more digest configurability) where B declines and marks the competitive audit [NEEDS INPUT]; A adds a useful 'Not being decided Thursday' scope-fence, a five-option alternatives table, and a sharper meta-critique that logins are themselves a proxy and renewal would be the better outcome metric. Against that, A asserts 'table stakes in this category' in the body and leans on it in §8 while conceding in its own Stress Test that it never verified anything beyond Asana. Demerits run the other way too: B invents a meeting date and gets it wrong — it stamps 'Executive Review — Thursday 17 Sep 2026' on the header from an assumed 'today is Wed 16 Sep 2026'; the day-of-week math is internally right but the actual date is 20 Sep 2026, making Thursday the 24th. A deliberately avoided this (its assumption 4 treats Week 1/2/4 as relative to build completion, not calendar dates), so B has a visible error in an exec-facing title, in a doc that explicitly promises not to invent facts the source lacks. B's §5 also runs slightly deeper into engineering detail than an exec needs (SMTP error code, header-vs-footer RFC mechanics), which cuts against expectation 3, though B justifies it with the blast-radius argument and pre-empts the objection in its Stress Test. Both outputs pass all four expectations, so expectations are not the discriminator here; the rubric is. Net: A has the higher-value single insight and did more real research; B is the better-built decision document — ask at the top, every ask decidable, a cleaner hypothesis spine, and more precisely sourced risk. For a doc whose entire brief is 'this is for the exec review on Thursday', B edges it.

verification_notes.arithmetic_check: Ran independently rather than trusting the output. A's compounding claim is correct: 0.995^52 = 0.77055, i.e. ~22.9% of the list gone within a year, matching A's '~23%' and '0.995^52 approximately 0.77'. A's companion figure also checks out: 0.999^52 = 0.94930, ~5.1% at a 0.10% rate, matching its '~5%'. Both documents' '~30% of the gap' is correct (0.7 / 2.3 = 30.4%), and '~480/year' from 40 tickets/month is correct. B carries the <0.5% per-send figure forward but never compounds it, so it makes no comparable claim to check.
verification_notes.date_check: B asserts 'Today is Wed 16 Sep 2026' and titles the doc 'Thursday 17 Sep 2026'. The day-of-week mapping is internally correct (16 Sep 2026 is a Wednesday, 17 Sep a Thursday), but the actual current date is 20 Sep 2026 (a Sunday), which puts the real Thursday at 24 Sep. B flagged it as an assumption with a stated consequence, which mitigates but does not remove the error. A stamped no date at all and reasoned explicitly that the source's Week 1/2/4 are relative to build completion.
